title: Real-world upper-limb use: the use ratio and magnitude ratio as a capacity-performance gap, on real dual-arm accelerometry

dataset.name: Daily and Sports Activities Data Set (DSADS)
dataset.record: subject p1, 19 daily/sports activities x 60 five-second segments; right-arm and left-arm accelerometer units @ 25 Hz (acc in m/s^2 -> g)
dataset.citation: Barshan B, Altun K. Daily and Sports Activities Data Set. UCI Machine Learning Repository. doi:10.24432/C5C59F (CC-BY 4.0).

proposition: Capacity (what an arm CAN do, measured in the clinic) and performance (what it ACTUALLY does in daily life) are different things; the wearable use ratio and magnitude ratio quantify the gap. On real dual-arm accelerometry from a healthy person the ecosystem recovers the SYMMETRIC reference: during activity both arms are used with near-equal magnitude -- every one of the 14 dynamic activities has |magnitude ratio| < 0.5 (max 0.34, mean 0.12) and use ratio 1.0, overall magnitude ratio -0.05 (0 = symmetric). This symmetry is the healthy baseline against which the stroke affected/unaffected asymmetry (use ratio << 1, magnitude ratio strongly negative) is read.

claims.statement: overall use ratio across all 19 activities (1 = symmetric arm use)
overall magnitude ratio (log right/left activity; 0 = symmetric)
activities in which both arms are actively used (use ratio == 1)
largest per-activity |magnitude ratio| among dynamic activities (all < 0.5 = symmetric)
mean per-activity |magnitude ratio| among dynamic activities

validation.reference: Healthy bilateral symmetry (Bailey/Lang/Uswatte accelerometry framework): in the absence of impairment the two arms are used with near-equal magnitude, so the use ratio is ~1 and the magnitude ratio ~0 -- the symmetric baseline against which the affected/unaffected asymmetry of stroke (use ratio << 1, magnitude ratio strongly negative) is measured
validation.data: REAL -- DSADS (UCI #256), one healthy subject, dual right-arm/left-arm accelerometers @ 25 Hz across 19 activities
validation.note: The reproducible result is the SYMMETRY: on real dual-arm data from a healthy person, whenever the arms are actually in use both are used near-equally -- every one of the 14 dynamic activities has |magnitude ratio| < 0.5 (max 0.34 basketball, mean 0.12) and use ratio 1.0, and the overall magnitude ratio is -0.05. This recovers the healthy reference the metric is built on. Two honest-scope caveats: (1) the static activities (sitting/standing/lying, use ratio ~0) have essentially motionless arms, where the magnitude ratio is noise-dominated and the use ratio is undefined-by-inactivity, not asymmetry -- correctly excluded from the symmetry claim; (2) the canonical use ratio is a whole-DAY free-living measure -- our 19-activity lab set is not a free-living day, so the overall 0.864 is a lab-activity number pulled down only by the static activities, not a free-living use ratio. The CLINICAL application -- the affected/unaffected use ratio and the capacity-performance gap in stroke -- needs bilateral-WRIST clinical recordings (e.g. NICHD DASH), which are DUA-gated, not freely public; this case demonstrates the METHOD recovers the symmetric reference on the freely public dual-arm data available.

open_questions.q: The clinical capacity-performance gap -- affected-arm use ratio well below 1 and a strongly negative magnitude ratio in stroke/CP -- needs bilateral-WRIST recordings from an impaired cohort (e.g. NICHD DASH); those datasets are data-use-agreement gated, not freely public, so this case validates the method against the healthy SYMMETRIC reference and documents the clinical asymmetry as the target application. Documented, not escalated.
